amortized: Average cost per operation over a sequence of operations, even if some individual operations are expensive. E.g. dynamic array resizing is O(1) amortized.
tail latency: Latency at the high end of a distribution (e.g. p99, p999). Even rare slow responses matter at scale.
idempotent: An operation that produces the same result regardless of how many times it's applied. Safe to retry.
memoization: Caching the result of a function call so the same inputs return the cached result instead of recomputing.
hashing: Mapping data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values using a hash function. Used in hash tables, checksums, bloom filters.
collision: When two distinct keys map to the same hash bucket. Handled via chaining or open addressing.
sharding: Partitioning data across multiple nodes so each node holds a subset. Enables horizontal scaling.
replication: Keeping copies of data on multiple nodes for fault tolerance and read throughput.
consensus: Agreement among distributed nodes on a single value, despite failures. E.g. Raft, Paxos.
eventual consistency: A consistency model where replicas converge to the same value given enough time and no new updates.
strong consistency: Every read reflects the most recent write. Requires coordination across replicas.
linearizability: The strongest consistency guarantee: operations appear instantaneous and in real-time order.
backpressure: A mechanism where a consumer signals a producer to slow down to avoid being overwhelmed.
throughput: The amount of work completed per unit of time. E.g. requests per second.
latency: Time taken to complete a single operation from start to finish.
big-o: Asymptotic notation describing the upper bound on an algorithm's time or space complexity as input grows.
recursion: A function that calls itself with a smaller subproblem until reaching a base case.
dynamic programming: Breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems, solving each once, and storing results to avoid recomputation.
greedy: An algorithm strategy that makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it leads to a global optimum.
divide and conquer: Recursively splitting a problem into independent subproblems, solving them, then combining results.
invariant: A condition that remains true throughout the execution of a program or loop.
predicate: A boolean-valued function or condition used to test a property.
heap: A tree-based data structure satisfying the heap property: parent ≥ children (max-heap) or parent ≤ children (min-heap).
trie: A tree where each node represents a character prefix. Enables O(m) string lookups where m is key length.
bloom filter: A probabilistic data structure that tests set membership. May produce false positives, never false negatives.
consistent hashing: A hashing scheme where adding/removing nodes minimizes key remapping. Used in distributed caches.
load balancing: Distributing incoming requests across multiple servers to avoid hotspots.
cache eviction: The process of removing entries from a cache when capacity is reached. Common policies: LRU, LFU, FIFO.
lru: Least Recently Used - evicts the item that was accessed furthest in the past.
two-pointer: A technique using two indices that move through a data structure, often from opposite ends, to solve problems in O(n).
monotonic stack: A stack kept strictly increasing or decreasing by popping elements that violate the order before pushing. Finds next-greater/smaller elements in O(n) total.
sliding window: A contiguous subrange over a sequence, expanded and contracted with two pointers to avoid re-scanning. Turns O(n²) brute force into O(n).
prefix sum: A precomputed running total, `pref[i] = pref[i-1] + arr[i]`, letting any range sum be answered in O(1) by subtraction.
topological order: A linear ordering of a DAG's nodes such that every edge points from an earlier node to a later one. Undefined if the graph has a cycle.
cycle detection: Determining whether a graph contains a cycle - a back edge in DFS for directed graphs, or a union-find same-root check for undirected ones.
load factor: The ratio of stored entries to bucket count in a hash table. High load factor increases collision rate and triggers a resize.
tombstone: A marker left in place of a deleted entry so lookups/traversals don't break, cleaned up later by compaction or a resize.
cache-friendly: Memory access patterns that exploit spatial/temporal locality (e.g. contiguous arrays) so the CPU cache holds the working set, avoiding slow main-memory fetches.
pointer chasing: Following a chain of memory addresses (e.g. a linked list) where each dereference is a potential cache miss, since the next address isn't known until the previous one is read.
call stack: The stack of active function-call frames; each recursive call pushes a frame, consuming O(depth) space until it returns.
exchange argument: A proof technique for greedy correctness: show any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without making it worse.
articulation point: A node whose removal disconnects the graph (or a subtree of it) - found via DFS low-link values in O(V + E).
sentinel: A dummy value or node placed at a boundary (e.g. a linked-list dummy head, or `pref[0] = 0`) to eliminate special-case edge checks.
horizontal scaling: Adding more machines to handle load, as opposed to making one machine bigger (vertical scaling). The standard distributed-systems scaling path.
vertical scaling: Increasing a single machine's resources (CPU, RAM) to handle more load, as opposed to adding more machines (horizontal scaling). Hits a hard ceiling.
fan-out: One write or event triggering many downstream writes/reads (e.g. a tweet fanning out to all followers' timelines). The scaling bottleneck in push-based systems.
thundering herd: Many clients simultaneously retrying or requesting the same resource after a cache expiry or outage, overwhelming the backend all at once.
circuit breaker: A pattern that stops calling a failing downstream service after a threshold of errors, failing fast instead of piling up timeouts, then probes for recovery.
idempotency key: A client-supplied unique token attached to a request so a retried request is recognized and not applied twice.
leader election: The process by which distributed nodes agree on a single coordinator, used to serialize writes or break ties. Core to Raft/Paxos and many primary-replica systems.
split-brain: A failure mode where a network partition causes two nodes to both believe they're the leader, each accepting writes - a correctness hazard in leader-election systems.
quorum: The minimum number of nodes that must agree for a read or write to be considered successful, ensuring overlap between read and write sets in a replicated system.
write amplification: When one logical write triggers multiple physical writes (e.g. LSM-tree compaction, SSD garbage collection), degrading throughput and device lifespan.
back-of-the-envelope: A rough, order-of-magnitude capacity estimate (QPS, storage, bandwidth) done early in a system-design discussion to sanity-check an approach before designing in detail.
